title: Cache requirements and scope
idea: Scoping a cache system means fixing its operations, its size limit, its eviction and expiry rules, and saying out loud what v1 does not do.
points: Callers need `get`, `put` and `remove` on keys, each in O(1) average time.
The cache holds at most capacity entries; a policy picks what leaves.
Entries may carry a time-to-live, and hits and misses are counted.
Many threads share one cache, so every operation must stay correct.

hero.title: What the cache does in v1

edges.caption: A read returns the value, or a miss the caller must handle by loading from the source.
A write stores a value. Writing an existing key replaces it and refreshes its place.
When the source data changes, the caller removes the key so nobody reads the old value.

edges.label: if full
edges.caption: A put into a full cache first evicts one key. The eviction policy decides which.

edges.label: checks
edges.caption: A read of an entry past its time-to-live counts as a miss and drops the entry.

edges.label: counts
edges.caption: Each read adds to hits or misses, so you can tell whether the cache earns its memory.
Surviving restarts and sharing across servers wait for a later version. Name them so the cut is clear.

code.title: Scope as an enum
code.caption: Each requirement is tagged functional or non-functional, and v1 is one explicit range of the enum.

walk.text: v1 is the range from GET to THREAD_SAFE. Anything after it is out.
Print each requirement with an IN or OUT tag and its kind.
Six functional needs: the three operations, eviction, expiry and statistics.
Three qualities: constant-time operations, a hard size bound, thread safety.
Persistence and clustering are listed on purpose, so the cut is visible.

pitfalls: Ask for the capacity unit early: entry count and bytes need different designs.
Agree on stale reads: say how old a cached value may be.
Never promise a distributed cache in v1 unless the interviewer asks for it.

quiz.q: Which v1 decision shapes the cache classes the most?
options: Choosing Redis as the backing store
A hard capacity with a pluggable eviction policy
Writing entries to disk on every put
quiz.why: A bounded size forces an eviction rule. Making that rule pluggable creates the EvictionPolicy interface the rest of the design depends on.

takeaway: Fix operations, capacity, eviction, expiry and thread safety before drawing classes.

starters: Should capacity count entries or bytes in an interview answer?
